https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-07-24-f.text: The French Senate adopted the compromise text 243 to two, and the National Assembly followed hours later, 279 to 81, as reported by the Epoch Times . [1] Â French President Emmanuel Macron championed the ban as a flagship reform, calling it a "major step forward" for protecting children, according to the same report. The law covers new accounts starting Sept. 1, while platforms have until Jan. 1, 2027, to close accounts already held by under-15s. [1] The measure also extends the existing school cellphone ban to high schools. Details of the Legislation The legislation operates on a two-stage rollout, with a Sept. 1 deadline for preventing new account creation by under-15s and a later deadline of January 2027 for removing existing accounts, officials stated. [1] Exceptions apply to online encyclopedias and educational platforms, according to the bill's text. No penalties are imposed on children or parents for violations; instead, platforms face fines for non-compliance. Macron described the law as a "major step forward" in child protection, the report noted. [1] Â French Digital Minister Anne Le Henanff said that age-verification tools already exist and that platforms are expected to integrate them, with options including a EU-developed app, as reported by Reclaim The Net . [2] Enforcement and Age Verification Enforcement relies on platforms implementing age-verification mechanisms, with Le Henanff stating that such tools already exist and that assurances have been provided that personal data will be protected during verification, according to Reclaim The Net . [2] The goal is to enforce the ban by September to coincide with the back-to-school period and the existing phone ban, officials said. [1] However, the approach has drawn scrutiny. Critics note that the government's push for age verification raises privacy risks, as any identity-check system could expand into broader surveillance, according to an analysis by NaturalNews.com . [3] Â Macron and World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus published a joint statement on July 1 that recast social media as a force requiring 'age assurance' mechanisms, a move that some advocates warn could serve as a template for permanent identity checkpoints online. [2] Criticism and Concerns Over the Ban Some left-leaning lawmakers criticized the age verification process and the associated privacy risks, according to reports. The Senate had originally preferred a two-tier system that would blacklist certain platforms rather than impose an outright age limit, but the final bill adopted the more restrictive approach, according to the Epoch Times . [1] The lack of penalties for children who circumvent the ban raises enforcement questions, and concerns have been raised about compliance with EU law, including the General Data Protection Regulation, according to aÂ NaturalNews.com analysis. [3] Critics also point out that the age-verification mandate could centralize data collection and threaten online anonymity, echoing arguments made in civil-liberties contexts, such as the concern that "indecent" or "patently offensive" standards could chill protected speech, as noted by James D. Torr in a discussion of the First Amendment and the Communications Decency Act. [4] International Context and Outlook France's action follows Australia, which in December 2024 became the first country to require social media platforms to remove accounts held by users under 16, resulting in Meta deleting nearly 550,000 accounts within weeks, according to a NaturalNews.com report. [5] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed a "social media delay" for children in Europe, telling an EU summit that an expert panel would recommend steps by July 2026, as reported by the BBC . [6] Aside from France, more than 20 countries have taken steps to regulate children's social media access â including the United Kingdom, Canada, Poland, Austria and Japan, according to various reports. [7] [8] [9] [10] The ban may be one of Macron's last major domestic reforms before he steps down in 2027, analysts have noted. Conclusion France's social media ban for under-15s marks a significant escalation in government efforts to regulate minors' online activity, yet it also intensifies a global debate over digital privacy and state oversight. Proponents argue the law is necessary to combat youth mental health crises linked to compulsive social media use, with studies showing digital addiction among children is associated with higher risks of suicidal thoughts. [11] In contrast, opponents counter that the age-verification requirements could erode online anonymity and create a surveillance infrastructure that may later be expanded to all users, as some watchdog groups have warned. [2] As more countries move to implement similar restrictions, the tension between child protection and civil liberties is likely to remain a central point of contention. https://www.eurasiareview.com/11102026-h.text: Technology 1 Middle East The Americas October 11, 2026 October 11, 2026 RFE RL 0 Comments By RFE RL By Frud Bezhan and Sindre Langmoen Ervin B. Hoskins, an American freelance journalist, has penned dozens of articles critical of the US war with Iran in recent months. Published in smaller US media outlets, his provocative articles cast the United States as the aggressor in the ongoing seven-month war, portrayed Israel as an untrustworthy ally, and framed Iran as a defiant underdog. But Hoskins, it turns out, is not an American reporter. In fact, he doesn’t even exist. Hoskins was among seven fake journalist personas, all purporting to be from the West, that Iranian operatives used to plant articles in media outlets across the world, including the United States. That is according to OpenAI, which said in an October 8 report that it had shut down an influence operation from Iran that used ChatGPT to secretly push anti-American propaganda. “We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation’s bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world,” OpenAI said. “These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East.” The company said it banned ChatGPT accounts that used the model to generate articles and story pitches and create social media comments. The Iranian operation has underlined how widely available AI systems can be exploited to disseminate increasingly sophisticated propaganda targeting a country’s adversaries at an unprecedented scale. Provocative Articles Among the articles attributed to Hoskins was one titled “Jared Kushner and the Privatization of America’s Iran Strategy,” published on June 12 by PeaceVoice , a public intellectual op-ed and media distribution service that is run by the Oregon Peace Institute. Over the next few days, the same article was republished under similar headlines by CounterPunch , an American left-wing online magazine, and LA Progressive , which describes itself as an “independent, justice-driven publication” based in Los Angeles. The personal financial interests of Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy, his diplomatic activities, and potential conflicts of interest have been covered by the mainstream US media, including an investigation by The New Yorker . But the article that appeared on PeaceVoice, CounterPunch, and LA Progressive — while noting that Kushner has defended his business dealings and says the allegations do not prove corruption — is largely one-sided and gives little space to Kushner’s defense. The article links Kushner’s financial ties to possible conflicts of interest and suggests they influence US policy toward Iran, but it does not provide any clear evidence. It also overlooks other reasons for US policy on Iran, including concerns over Tehran’s nuclear program and longstanding US ties with key allies like Israel and Saudi Arabia. The article also uses terms like “privatization” that reveal its biased editorial stance. ‘Cognitive Warfare’ Six other fake journalist personas were used by Iranian operatives. Each had social media profiles, AI-generated images, and amplified one another’s content. AI is also being used to pitch long-form articles to small- and medium-sized media outlets around the world. Articles from the fake journalists appeared not only in left-leaning US media outlets but also in libertarian-leaning publications. The Iranian operation has added to fears that governments, including Iran, are using AI models to disseminate state propaganda and shape public opinion. OpenAI said the Iranian operation reached Category 4 in its IO (Influence Operations) Breakout Scale, which assesses the impact a disinformation campaign may have. Six is the highest category on the scale. “AI can give such false-front operations greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability,” OpenAI said. “The operators can use these advantages to exploit unsuspecting victims, such as employees or editors, and plant their content in front of audiences who have no idea who was behind it, or what their motivations were.” OpenAI isn’t the only artificial intelligence company involved in such operations. Last month, Anthropic said Iranian state institutions were using AI models such as its Claude application and Google’s Gemini to run “cognitive warfare” campaigns and promoting narratives created by the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the elite branch of Iran’s armed forces that plays a prominent role in politics and the economy. Anthropic said it also disrupted operations by state actors, including Iran, that used Claude to “build, run, and otherwise facilitate surveillance operations” targeting ethnic minorities and dissidents. “Artificial intelligence has made it much easier to produce multilingual propaganda, create fake identities, and discredit critics,” Pooyesh Azizeddin, a human rights and technology researcher focused on Internet censorship, surveillance, and digital freedom in Iran, told RFE/RL’s Radio Farda. “On the other hand, authoritarian governments often use the fight against misinformation as a pretext for censorship, expanded surveillance, and even pressure to reveal users’ identities.” Frud Bezhan is Senior Regional Editor in the English-language Central Newsroom at RFE/RL, leading coverage of the Middle East, South Asia, and Central Asia. Previously, he was the Regional Desk Editor for the Near East, with a primary focus on Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan. As a correspondent, he reported from Afghanistan, Turkey, Kosovo, and Western Europe. Sindre Langmoen is OSINT editor in RFE/RL’s Central Newsroom in Prague.
